Local MemorySmith tool results: Found 3 items. memory:project-wiki-hybrid-search-rrf — Hybrid Search With RRF: Combines Lucene.NET lexical index with ONNX semantic embeddings via reciprocal rank fusion. memory:project-wiki-onnx-semantic-embeddings — ONNX Semantic Embeddings: MiniLM-L6-v2, 384-dim vectors, cosine similarity scoring. memory:project-wiki-mcp-search-tools-current — MCP Search Tools: Exposes lexical, semantic, hybrid, unified, and context-pack retrieval modes.

Hybrid search in MemorySmith runs two retrieval passes in parallel. The lexical pass uses a Lucene.NET index for exact term matching, while the semantic pass encodes the query with MiniLM-L6-v2 into a 384-dimensional vector and scores candidates by cosine similarity. Results from both passes are merged using reciprocal rank fusion (RRF), which re-scores each candidate based on its rank position in each list rather than raw scores, producing a balanced final ranking. The MCP layer exposes this as one of several retrieval modes including a dedicated hybrid endpoint.

The /admin workbench itself gates access to user management, OAuth configuration, and model profile editing behind this same Admin claim.

What's the difference between unified and context-pack?

Based on the knowledge base, the MCP layer exposes five retrieval modes. Unified search fans out across all available modes and merges results into a single ranked list, making it the broadest single query. Context-pack is more specialized: it takes search roots (or explicit memory IDs), follows backlinks, and assembles a bounded output bundle sized for LLM consumption. Use unified when you want breadth; use context-pack when you need a self-contained context window for an agent.

What exactly is Reciprocal Rank Fusion?

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the algorithm MemorySmith uses to combine results from two different search strategies into a single ranked list. The BM25 keyword scorer and the ONNX semantic embedding scorer each produce their own ranked results. RRF merges these by assigning each result a score based on the reciprocal of its rank in each list, then summing those scores to produce a final ordering. This means a result that ranks highly in both keyword and semantic search will appear near the top of the combined output.
